Adaptive immune response and regulation concerning T and B cells
label_2: Module description: Adaptive immunity refers to a highly specific immune response that plays a critical role in eliminating pathogens. This system relies primarily on B and T lymphocytes, which express diverse antigen-specific receptors capable of recognizing unique molecular features of foreign invaders. During infection, dendritic cells (DCs) act as peripheral sentinels that capture and process pathogens into antigenic peptides. These antigens are then presented to T cells via major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules. Upon recognizing a cognate antigen and receiving costimulatory signals, such as CD28 engagement with B7.1/B7.2, T cells become activated, initiating a cascade of intracellular signaling events. These cascades involve protein tyrosine kinases, phosphatases, GTP-binding proteins, and adaptor proteins, which together orchestrate T-cell proliferation, cytokine secretion, and differentiation into effector cells. B cells, which mediate humoral immunity, recognize antigens through their B cell receptor (BCR), a complex composed of membrane-bound immunoglobulin molecules and the signaling subunits Ig-α and Ig-β. Following antigen binding, signaling is initiated through the activation of key protein tyrosine kinases, including the SRC-family kinase LYN, SYK, and the TEC-family kinase BTK. Downstream signaling molecules such as phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and phospholipase C-γ2 (PLC-γ2) are activated, ultimately leading to the expression of immediate early genes. These transcriptional changes promote B cell proliferation, differentiation, antibody production, and further immune responses. Together, the TCR and BCR signaling pathways are central to the adaptive immune system, coordinating the cellular and humoral arms to achieve a robust and specific defense against pathogens.
